Thanks again for the demo last week. Two follow-ups from our engineering and procurement teams as we scope the pilot:

1) Our workflows frequently send ~12k token contexts (search results + patient notes) and then stream short (200–400 token) model outputs. How will those long context pieces be accounted for? 3) Rounding/minimums: procurement wants concrete examples we can show legal — e.g., if a single request includes 12,345 input tokens and 300 output tokens, what line items appear on the invoice? Also, are there per-request minimums, and how do you round long contexts?

We'd like to lock these rules into the pilot SOW so customers don't get surprised. Can you send a brief worked example and any adjustable pilot levers (slab size, prefix-credit, pilot discount)?

Hi Liam —

Thanks — great questions. Summary up-front: by default we bill (1) input tokens, (2) output tokens, and (3) a context-allocation slab for large unique context material. For your pilot we can adjust the slab size and add an explicit prefix-reuse credit. Below are short explanations plus an example. Karthik will follow up with the detailed math and an example invoice.

How it works (short):
- Per-request token accounting = input_tokens + output_tokens (billed per-token at the published rate).
- For large contexts (unique context > slab_threshold) we apply a context-allocation slab. The slab is charged to account for memory/KV allocation and sustained KV residency; slabs are sized to balance cost predictability and backend allocation overhead.
- Prefix-reuse credit: when a request reuses an existing cached prefix within a reuse window, we apply a credit to the billed context slab to avoid double-charging for identical prefixes.

Default values (hosted):
- slab_threshold = 4,096 tokens
- slab_size = 4,096 tokens (we charge up to the next slab for the newly observed unique context)
- reuse_window = 1 hour (hits within window get reuse credit)
- per_request_min = 12 tokens (very small generated responses are floored; this is to prevent microbilling noise)

Example (default rules):
Request A: input = 12,345 tokens (unique), output = 300 tokens
- Input tokens billed: 12,345
- Output tokens billed: 300
- Context slabs: ceil(12,345 / 4,096) = 4 slabs -> billed context allocation = 4 * 4,096 = 16,384 tokens
- Effective billed tokens (line items): input 12,345, output 300, context-allocation 16,384 (this is a one-time allocation charge while the unique context is resident)

Notes:
- If subsequent requests within the reuse_window reuse large prefixes from Request A, we apply a configurable prefix credit (percentage reduction) against the incremental slab charge.
- Streaming responses are billed exactly like non-streamed: tokens emitted are counted as output tokens as they are produced. The context-allocation is assessed against the unique input at the time it is first observed.

Attached is a short billing-spec (billing-spec-v2.pdf) and Karthik will attach an example invoice breakdown.

If you want, we can make the pilot-friendly adjustments: reduce slab_size to 1,024 and increase prefix-credit to 40% for the pilot period. That tends to make invoices look much closer to actual incremental work for customers who reuse large prefixes frequently.

Best,
Naomi Feldman
Sales Operations | Redwood Inference

Hi Liam / Naomi —

Quick technical note to make the math deterministic for legal/procurement.

Principles:
- We charge for unique context material the first time it is observed and allocated into the serving cache. That allocation is the context-allocation slab.
- Subsequent requests that reference existing KV entries do not re-charge the full slab; they either (a) incur only input/output token costs for deltas, or (b) if they add new unique context beyond current slabs, we charge additional slabs for the incremental unique tokens.

Formalized (pilot-friendly formula):
- unique_new = max(0, total_unique_context_tokens_seen_by_request - existing_allocated_tokens_for_session)
- slabs_added = ceil(unique_new / slab_size)
- billed_context_increment = slabs_added * slab_size
- billed_tokens_for_request = input_tokens + output_tokens + billed_context_increment

Example using Naomi's numbers and pilot slab_size = 1,024 with prefix-credit = 40%:
- Request A (first observation): input 12,345, output 300
  - unique_new = 12,345 -> slabs_added = ceil(12,345 / 1,024) = 13 -> billed_context_increment = 13 * 1,024 = 13,312
  - billed_tokens = 12,345 + 300 + 13,312 = 25,957 tokens (line items: input 12,345; output 300; context allocation 13,312)
- Request B (within reuse_window, reuses prefix of 10,000 tokens and adds 2,000 new tokens):
  - existing_allocated_tokens_for_session = 13,312 (from A)
  - total_unique_context_tokens_seen_by_request = 10,000 + 2,000 = 12,000 -> unique_new = max(0,12,000 - 13,312) = 0 -> slabs_added = 0 -> billed_context_increment = 0
  - billed_tokens = input_tokens + output_tokens (no additional context allocation)

Prefix-credit behavior:
- The prefix-credit is applied only to the slab charge when we detect repeated identical prefixes across requests (byte-equality within the reuse_window). With a 40% prefix-credit, a repeated prefix that otherwise would have caused a small slab increment would receive a 40% reduction of that increment.

Edge cases:
- Short-lived micro-requests (< per_request_min tokens) are floored to per_request_min.
- If a session's cached allocation is garbage-collected (evicted), a later request that references the same prefix will look like a new allocation and be charged accordingly. Eviction windows are a function of account activity and are included in the billing spec.

Attached: example-invoice.csv with a row-by-row walk-through of the two-request example above.

Happy to walk this through with your legal/procurement team. If you prefer stricter predictability we can also convert the context allocation into a monthly reserved seat commitment for the pilot.

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Applied ML & Inference Optimization | Redwood Inference
